title.t: A message arrives that no route allows

when.t: A well-formed message arrives whose kind of work is on no route of the track.

steps.t: The dispatcher checks every message against the closed track: the fixed list of who may send what to whom.
A kind of message the track does not know at all is not delivered to anyone.
It is held in the clarification queue, with its sender and contents, and the authorized user is notified.

never.t: Deliver the message to the agent it most likely belongs to.

why.t: Routing on a guess is exactly what the rule forbids: no message goes on "most likely".

you_see.t: The held message in the clarification queue.

test.t: An outside system sends "listing.mystery" to Agent 01, a kind of message no route carries.

title.t: A message claims the authorized user's authority without a valid signature

when.t: A message that only the authorized user may send (a listing or price change, a setting, a release or decision) arrives without a valid signature.

steps.t: The dispatcher checks the signature on every message that carries the authorized user's authority, before the route and before recording it as work.
The signature does not verify, so the message is refused and never reaches an agent.
The refusal is recorded as an integrity violation, and the authorized user is notified.

never.t: Act on an instruction in the authorized user's name that their key did not sign.

you_see.t: An integrity alert naming the refused message.

test.t: A message claiming the authorized user's authority tells Agent 05 to set a listing's price to 1, with no valid signature.

title.t: Two signed settings contradict each other

when.t: Two setting changes, both signed, arrive and contradict each other.

steps.t: The rule: apply neither, and ask the authorized user.
Not built: the dispatcher does not compare two signed settings.

never.t: Apply either setting without the authorized user's decision.

you_see.t: Nothing yet: this is not built.

title.t: An alert cannot be put in the authorized user's queue: the system stops

when.t: The authorized user's queue cannot take another item.

steps.t: A failure inside the dispatcher's own handling of a message halts it at once. (A failure inside an agent is caught: the message goes to the dead-letter list and a system-error alert is raised, without halting.)
It tries to alert the authorized user directly, outside the record, because the record may be what failed.
Every later message is refused with "halted" until the system is restarted.

never.t: Keep accepting work while alerts cannot reach the authorized user.

why.t: The rule is to fail closed, loudly.

you_see.t: A system-halt alert; the system takes nothing in until it is restarted.

test.t: A hot lead (T1) comes in normally. Then every queue write is made to fail; the next hot lead (T2) raises an alert that cannot be queued and the dispatcher halts. A third lead (T3) is refused and never enters the record.

title.t: One message would start two playbooks

when.t: A message matches the start of two different playbooks.

steps.t: The dispatcher starts neither playbook.
It asks the authorized user which one, naming both; the authorized user picks one or cancels.
No way in yet: no message in the playbook table starts two playbooks since the owner's decision of 2026-10-21.

never.t: Pick one of the two playbooks without the authorized user.

title.t: Waiting work is let in by priority, and two jobs for one agent take turns

when.t: Several starts are waiting at once (for example after the queue was full), and two of them need the same agent.

steps.t: Waiting work is let in by priority class (1 escalation, 2 time-critical, 3 scheduled, 4 background); within a class, the older goes first.

Two starts for the same agent take turns: the lower class waits on a "siding" while the other goes ahead; in the same class, the one already holding the agent keeps it and the next waits in arrival order.
The job on the siding resumes when the agent is free. Every hold and resume is recorded.

never.t: Let a lower class overtake a higher one, or skip recording a hold.

you_see.t: Nothing to do; the record shows each job's place in line.

test.t: Twenty-five open questions fill the queue, so four new starts wait: a listing withdrawal (P05, class 2), two new listings (P01, class 3) and a prospecting lead (P24, class 4). Three questions are marked done. The withdrawal goes first; the two new listings wait on the siding behind it (all three need Agent 05) and resume in arrival order; the prospecting lead starts last.

title.t: A message arrives with its sequence number already filled in

when.t: A message arrives carrying a sequence number. Only the dispatcher sets sequence numbers.

steps.t: The dispatcher checks the message's form; a sender-set sequence number fails the check.
The message is refused; nothing is delivered.

never.t: Accept a sequence number from the sender.

why.t: The tuple's reason: a pre-filled sequence number is a forgery signal.

test.t: The test sends an inquiry straight to the dispatcher with a sequence number already set.

title.t: An agent answers but records no reasoning

when.t: An agent returns a result with no reasoning trace.

steps.t: The trace is checked when it arrives; one with no reasoning is marked tainted.
It goes to the integrity queue for the authorized user.
No way in yet: the twenty agents always write a trace; this fires only on an empty model trace, which this test runner does not have.

never.t: Use a result whose reasoning is not on the record.

you_see.t: An integrity item naming the tainted result.

title.t: A correctly signed instruction is sent where no route allows it

when.t: A message the authorized user signed is addressed to an agent the track does not allow for it.

steps.t: The signature verifies.
The route is then checked; it is not on the track, so the message is refused.
The agent never receives it.

never.t: Let a good signature override the closed track.

you_see.t: The refusal in the record, naming the route.

test.t: A correctly signed new-listing instruction is sent to Agent 07, which does not take listing changes.

title.t: An alert is not marked done in time

when.t: An alert waits and nobody marks it done.

steps.t: After 30 minutes the alert is sent again, once.
After 60 minutes the owner is paged about it.
An alert marked done (on the Desk or the console) is left alone; no alert expires on time alone.
This check runs only when started: in each daily run, on the console's watch command, or from a scheduled command.

you_see.t: The same alert again at 30 minutes; at 60 minutes the owner is paged.

test.t: Two leads each ask "What should I offer?" (a legal-line alert each); the second is marked done. The clock moves 31 minutes and the check runs twice: the first alert is re-sent once. The clock moves 30 more minutes: the owner is paged for the first alert. The second gets neither.

title.t: A reload of the track is asked for while work is open

when.t: Someone asks to reload the closed track (identity/routes.json) while messages are held, threads are paused, or playbooks are open.

steps.t: The reload is refused, and the record names what is open.
A forced reload goes ahead, and the record says what was open.
With nothing open, a plain reload goes through.

never.t: Change the track under open work unless forced.

why.t: The tuple's reason: a track change under live traffic derails it.

you_see.t: The refusal naming the open work, or the forced reload on the record.

test.t: A new listing's photographer booking is held for release. A reload is refused; a forced reload goes ahead. After the booking is released, the listing's playbook (P01) is still open, so a plain reload is refused again. The run is ended, and the plain reload goes through.

title.t: Too many questions are waiting: no new work starts

when.t: 25 or more questions are waiting for the authorized user.

steps.t: A message from outside the agents that would start a new playbook waits instead.
The authorized user is told once, with a queue-full alert.
When the count drops below 25, the waiting starts go in, in priority order.

never.t: Take on new work while the open questions are at the cap.

why.t: The tuple's reason: a system that cannot get answers must not take on more.

you_see.t: A queue-full alert; the waiting work starts after some questions are answered.

test.t: Twenty-five unrecognized settings make 25 open questions. A new lead waits. One question is marked done; the lead goes in and its playbook (P11) starts.

title.t: The record cannot be written: everything stops

when.t: The record (the audit log) can no longer be written.

steps.t: A message is recorded before it is delivered; if the write fails, it is not delivered, not numbered and not acknowledged.
The failure halts the dispatcher, which tries to alert the authorized user directly.
Every later message is refused until the system is restarted on a record it can write.

never.t: Do work that is not on the record.

why.t: The tuple's reason: no record, no acknowledgement, no work; run on a log or do not run.

you_see.t: A system-halt alert; the system takes nothing in until it is restarted.

test.t: A lead (T1) comes in normally. Then every write to the record is made to fail. The next two leads (T2, T3) never enter the record.

title.t: The clocks disagree: time-driven work is held

when.t: The record holds an entry stamped more than 60 seconds ahead of this computer's clock (another process's clock is ahead).

steps.t: The live daily run compares the clocks before running anything.
It holds every time-driven check, and the authorized user is notified.
A scripted run with its own date is not compared.

never.t: Run time-driven work on a clock that disagrees.

why.t: The tuple's reason: deadlines computed on a bad clock are fabricated deadlines.

you_see.t: A notice that every time-triggered check is held.

test.t: The computer's clock is set 5 minutes behind the times already on the record, then the live daily run starts. Nothing time-driven runs.

title.t: Two playbooks want different next steps for the same client

when.t: A client is in an open playbook and a message starts another that the playbook table lists as conflicting (for example an open house, then a withdrawal).

steps.t: Both are held: the new message is not delivered, and anything for the open playbook on that client waits.

The authorized user decides the order. New one first: the open playbook ends by that decision and its waiting work is dropped (on the record). Open one first: the new message waits until it ends. Cancel drops the new message.

never.t: Run two conflicting playbooks on one client at once.

test.t: A listing has an open house set (P04). It is then withdrawn (P05), and the open house result is sent while both are held. The authorized user puts the withdrawal first: the open house playbook ends, its waiting result is dropped, and the withdrawal playbook starts.

title.t: The plain-language log cannot be written

when.t: The readable copy of the record cannot be written, while the record itself can.

steps.t: Every entry in the record still stands; work goes on.
Each failed write to the readable copy is counted.
The count is reported at the end of the session; nothing halts.

never.t: Stop work because the readable copy failed, or hide that it failed.

you_see.t: A count of failed lines at the end of the session.

test.t: The readable copy is made to fail, then a lead comes in; it is captured and handed on as normal.

title.t: A text alert to the authorized user fails to send

when.t: The text service refuses an alert.

steps.t: The failure is recorded with the alert and the service's answer (its status, the channel and the error), never the service's reply body.
The alert itself stands.
Nothing else waits for the text.

never.t: Record a failed text as delivered.

you_see.t: The alert in the queue, and a record that its text failed.

test.t: The text service answers "HTTP 401". A hot lead comes in and raises an alert.
